bible_refs.note: νυνὶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτό, ἀλλ' ἡ οἰκοῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία.
Lemma: εἰ δὲ ὃ οὐ θέλω, τοῦτο ποιῶ, σύμφημι τῷ νόμῳ ὅτι καλός.
πόθεν πόλεμοι ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ πόθεν μάχαι; οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν, ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν ὑμῶν τῶν στρατευομένων ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν; introduced as 'the Savior's disciple'.
Lemma τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὐχ εὑρίσκω, then repeated with οὔ and 'and what follows'. Inline citation given once on the lemma.
εἰ δὲ ὃ οὐ θέλω ἐγώ, τοῦτο ποιῶ, οὐκέτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτό, ἀλλ' ἡ οἰκοῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία.
Lemma begins at the end of this section (εὑρίσκω ἄρα τὸν νόμον τῷ θέλοντι ἐμοί) and finishes in u05-rem-close (ποιεῖν τὸ καλόν, ὅτι ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται).

choices.english: the bonds and laws of their masters
choices.why: δεσμοῖς τοῖς τῶν κρατούντων … νόμοις rendered 'the bonds and laws of their masters'; the Greek may also be read as 'the binding laws'. Sense unchanged.
ἀλλ' ἦν ἐπ' αὐτῷ, φησί is an objector's reply (φησί with an implied subject), not Paul; rendered 'someone says'. Cyril then answers it (οὐκοῦν ἔστω …).
σάρξ rendered 'flesh' and νοῦς 'mind' consistently; θελήματα 'will' (collective) in the reins image.

παράκειται in Romans 7:18 (and in Cyril's τὸ παρακεῖσθαι … τὸ ἀγαθόν) reads 'lies close at hand', matching Romans 7:21 in u05-rem-close and the same verse in u06-open and u06-rem-early, so Paul's repeated verb reads the same across the book.

pass_a_gloss: [continuing u05-rem-early: worked the] sin, yet after this they are filled (μεμέστωνται) with dejection; to these, having grown weak all but unwillingly, it would befit (πρέποι) to say again: but now no longer I work it, but the sin dwelling (οἰκοῦσα) in me. Lemma: if what I do not will this I do, I agree (σύμφημι) with the law that it is good. Again he applies the exactness of contemplation to the nature of the body, and examines the power of the sicknesses in it naturally. For the appetites carrying off toward any passion whatever, and the charges of a pleasure-loving life, have the flesh as their spring; and to this the disciple of the Saviour confirms (ἐμπεδοῖ) us, saying: whence wars among you and whence fights? not from here, from your pleasures that make war in your members? Lemma: for to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. 'For to will,' he says, 'is present with me, but to accomplish the good, not,' and what follows; for a proof (ἀπόδειξιν) that the flesh is accused, in labour terribly with sin within itself, he wisely admits that the good lies close at hand (παράκειται) to us, but not also the being able to bring it through; for it forces the mind, not willing, into an unwilled turning aside. So as far as it came to what seemed good to it, it would be outside even sin; but since it endures a hard-to-escape overpowering, the cause would fittingly be not its own but of what overpowers. Therefore he says: if what I do not will I do, no longer I work it, but the indwelling sin. But someone might say: if some wicked barbarians, having ravaged a city or country, then taking some of the inhabitants as spear-won captives laid on them the yoke of slavery, and those suffering this yielded as of necessity to the bonds, the laws of the rulers, would they be worthy of reproach and indictment because they are neither superior to necessity nor eager to accomplish what is pleasant to themselves, disregarding the authority of those who had seized power? But no one, I think, would fittingly blame them; for not being allowed to be released they serve as slaves, and yield, as I said, to unwilled misfortunes; distressed that they are deprived of freedom, but, defeated (ἡττώμενοι) by necessity by the stronger, they serve not willingly. But if this is not far from what is reasonable, let the human mind be released from indictment over the sicknesses of the flesh. 'But it was in its power,' he says, 'not to choose (ἑλέσθαι) to act; for it holds the reins of the wills.' So let it be superior to overpowering and not tyrannized by sins. But if the nature of the flesh is hard to bear and not easy to meet, raising up against the mind untamed pleasure, and the law is more sluggish toward help—for it has not the power to put sins to death—no one would justly accuse it that it does not do the better, letting go the more shameful, even if perhaps it has the reins of the wills in us. Lemma: I find then the law, for me who wills… [continues in u05-rem-close]
pass_b_english: … sin, but afterward they are filled with dejection. It would be quite fitting for these people, who have grown weak almost against their will, to say in turn, “But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans 7:17).
“Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good” (Romans 7:16).

Again he turns the precision of his inquiry to the nature of the body, and examines the power of the sicknesses that are in it by nature. For the appetites that carry us off toward every kind of passion, and the faults of a pleasure-loving life, have their source in the flesh. The Savior’s disciple confirms us in this when he says, “Where do wars and where do quarrels among you come from? Do they not come from here, from your pleasures that wage war in your members?” (James 4:1).
“For willing lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good I do not find” (Romans 7:18).

“For willing,” he says, “lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not,” and so on. To show that the flesh stands accused, since it is in terrible labor with sin within itself, he wisely grants that the good lies close at hand for us, but not also the power to carry it through. For the flesh forces the mind, against its will, to turn aside where it does not wish to go. So as far as the mind’s own choice went, it would be free even of sin. But since it suffers an overpowering that is hard to escape, the blame would rightly belong not so much to the mind as to what overpowers it. That is why he says, “Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans 7:20).

But someone might say: suppose some wicked barbarians laid waste a city or a country, then took some of its inhabitants as captives of the spear and laid on them the yoke of slavery, and those who suffered this yielded by necessity to the bonds and laws of their masters. Would they deserve blame and indictment because they are not stronger than necessity, and do not strive to carry out what pleases themselves in defiance of the authority of those who have seized power over them? No one, I think, could fairly find fault with them. For they serve as slaves because they cannot be set free, and they yield, as I said, to misfortunes they did not want. They are distressed that they have been robbed of freedom, but, overcome by necessity by those who are stronger, they serve against their will. Now if this is not far from reason, let the human mind be acquitted of any charge over the sicknesses of the flesh.

“But it was in its power,” someone says, “not to choose to do it; for it holds the reins of its own will.” Then let it be stronger than that overpowering and free from the tyranny of sins. But if the nature of the flesh is hard to bear and hard to resist, stirring up untamed pleasure against the mind, and the law is too slow to help (for it does not have the power to put sins to death), no one could justly accuse the mind of failing to do the better thing and let go of the more shameful, even if it does perhaps hold the reins of the will within us.
“So I find this law: that when I want …” (Romans 7:21)

ἁμαρτίαν, κατηφείας γεμὴν μετὰ τοῦτο μεμέστωνται· τούτοις ἂν πρέποι καὶ μάλα
εἰκότως μονονουχὶ καὶ ἀβουλήτως ἠσθηνηκόσι τὸ φάναι δὴ πάλιν "Νυνὶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγὼ
κατεργάζομαι αὐτὸ, ἀλλ' ἡ "οἰκοῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία." Εἰ δὲ ὃ οὐ θέλω, τοῦτο ποιῶ,
σύμφημι τῷ νόμῳ ὅτι καλός.
Ἐνίησι πάλιν τῆς θεωρίας τὸ ἀκριβὲς τῇ τοῦ σώματος φύσει, καὶ τῶν ἐνόντων
αὐτῷ φυσικῶς ἀῤῥωστημάτων τὴν δύναμιν κατασκέπτεται. αἵ τε γὰρ ὀρέξεις αἱ πρὸς
πᾶν ὁτιοῦν ἀποκομίζουσαι τῶν παθῶν, καὶ τῆς φιληδόνου ζωῆς τὰ ἐγκλήματα, πηγὴν
ἔχουσι τὴν σάρκα· καὶ πρός γε τοῦτο ἡμᾶς ἐμπεδοῖ λέγων τοῦ Σωτῆρος ὁ μαθητής
"Πόθεν πόλε"μοι ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ πόθεν μάχαι; οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν, ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν "ὑμῶν τῶν
στρατευομένων ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν;" Τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ
κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν, οὐχ εὑρίσκω. Τὸ γὰρ θέλειν φησὶ παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ
κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ· καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς· εἰς ἀπόδειξιν τοῦ κατηγορεῖσθαι τὴν σάρκα
δεινῶς ὠδίνουσαν ἐν ἑαυτῇ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, παραδέχεται σοφῶς τὸ παρακεῖσθαι μὲν ἡμῖν
τὸ ἀγαθὸν, μὴ μὴν ἔτι καὶ τὸ δύνασθαι διαπεραίνειν αὐτό· καταβιάζεται γὰρ εἰς
ἀβούλητον ἐκτροπὴν καὶ οὐχ ἑκόντα τὸν νοῦν. οὐκοῦν 207 ὅσον ἧκεν εἴς γε τὸ αὐτῷ
δοκοῦν, ἦν ἂν ἔξω καὶ ἁμαρτίας· ἐπειδὴ δὲ δυσδιάφυκτον ὑπομένει πλεονεξίαν, εἴη ἂν
εἰκότως, οὐκ αὐτοῦ δὴ μᾶλλον, ἀλλὰ τοῦ πλεονεκτοῦντος ἡ αἰτία· ταύτῃτοί φησιν Εἰ δὲ
ὃ οὐ θέλω ἐγὼ, τοῦτο ποιῶ, οὐκέτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτὸ, ἀλλ' ἡ οἰκοῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ
ἁμαρτία. Εἴποι δὲ ἄν τις Ἆρα εἴ τινες τῶν ἀλιτηρίων βαρβάρων πόλιν ἢ χώραν
καταδῃώσαντες, εἶτα δορυκτήτους τῶν ἐνοικούντων ἑλόντες τινὰς τὸν τῆς δουλείας
αὐτῶν ἐπιτιθεῖεν ζυγόν· οἱ δὲ τοῦτο πεπονθότες ὡς ἐξ ἀναγκαίου δεσμοῖς τοῖς τῶν

14

κρατούντων εἴκοιεν νόμοις, μώμου καὶ γραφῆς εἶεν ἂν ἄξιοι, ὅτι μήτε ἀμείνους τῆς
ἀνάγκης εἰσὶ, μήτε μὴν τὸ σφίσιν αὐτοῖς ἡδὺ διαπεραίνειν σπουδάζουσι, τῆς τῶν
τετυραννηκότων ἀλογήσαντες ἐξουσίας; ἀλλ' οὐκ ἂν οἶμαί τις αὐτοὺς εἰκότως
διαμωμήσαιτο. οὐ γὰρ ἐξὸν ἀνεῖσθαι δουλεύουσιν, εἴκουσι δὲ ὡς ἔφην ταῖς ἀβουλήτοις
συμφοραῖς. ἀλύοντες μὲν ὅτι τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἐστέρηνται, τοῖς γεμὴν ἀλκιμοτέροις ἐξ
ἀνάγκης ἡττώμενοι καὶ οὐχ ἕκοντες δουλεύουσιν. ἀλλ' εἴπερ ἐστὶ τοῦτο τοῦ εἰκότος οὐ
μακρὰν, ἀπηλλάχθω γραφῆς ὁ ἀνθρώπινος νοῦς ἐπὶ τοῖς τῆς σαρκὸς ἀῤῥωστήμασιν.
ἀλλ' ἦν ἐπ' αὐτῷ, φησὶ, καὶ τὸ μὴ ἑλέσθαι δρᾶν· ἔχει γὰρ αὐτὸς τὰς τῶν θελημάτων
ἡνίας. οὐκοῦν ἔστω καὶ πλεονεξίας ἀμείνων καὶ ἀτυράννευτος ἁμαρτίαις. εἰ δὲ
δύσοιστος καὶ οὐκ εὐάντητος ἡ τῆς σαρκὸς φύσις, κατεξανιστᾶσα τῷ νῷ τὴν ἀτίθασον
ἡδονὴν, ἀργότερος δὲ πρὸς ἐπικουρίαν ὁ νόμος· οὐ γὰρ ἔχει τὸ δύνασθαι νεκροῦν
ἁμαρτίας· οὐκ ἂν ἐγκαλέσειέ τις δικαίως ὅτι μὴ δρᾷ τὸ ἀμεῖνον τὰ αἰσχίω μεθείς· κἂν εἰ
ἔχοι τυχὸν τὰς τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν θελημάτων ἡνίας. Εὑρίσκω ἄρα τὸν νόμον τῷ θέλοντι ἐμοὶ
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Consistency: Paul's verb παράκειται (Romans 7:18, and Cyril's τὸ παρακεῖσθαι … τὸ ἀγαθόν) was 'is present with me' here but 'lies close at hand' for the same verse in u06-open and u06-rem-early and for Romans 7:21 in u05-rem-close; Cyril's argument turns on the good and the evil both 'lying at hand', so the rendering is now the same throughout. No other change: the rest was checked clause by clause and is faithful (objector speaker, captives analogy, negations and agency correct); Romans 7:16, 7:17, 7:18, 7:20, 7:21 and James 4:1 verified.
Opening cut: ἁμαρτίαν completes ἐνηργήκασι τὴν at the end of u05-rem-early; leading ellipsis marks the join.
Closing cut: the Romans 7:21 lemma breaks after τῷ θέλοντι ἐμοί; trailing ellipsis, and the rest of the verse belongs to u05-rem-close.
The numeral 207 and the stray '14' are copy-text page markers and are not translated.
Source spelling ἠσθηνηκόσι read as ἠσθενηκόσι (perfect participle of ἀσθενέω, 'grown weak').

Subjects made explicit where the Greek leaves them to context: καταβιάζεται has 'the flesh' as subject and 'the mind' (τὸν νοῦν) as object; the following ἦν ἂν ἔξω καὶ ἁμαρτίας and αὐτοῦ refer to the mind. Rendering names 'the flesh' and 'the mind' for clarity, without adding new content.
δεσμοῖς τοῖς τῶν κρατούντων … νόμοις rendered 'the bonds and laws of their masters'; the Greek may also be read as 'the binding laws'. Sense unchanged.
ἀλλ' ἦν ἐπ' αὐτῷ, φησί is an objector's reply (φησί with an implied subject), not Paul; rendered 'someone says'. Cyril then answers it (οὐκοῦν ἔστω …).
πλεονεξία here is 'being overpowered, getting the upper hand' (cf. πλεονεκτούμενος earlier), not 'greed'.
σάρξ rendered 'flesh' and νοῦς 'mind' consistently; θελήματα 'will' (collective) in the reins image.

παράκειται in Romans 7:18 (and in Cyril's τὸ παρακεῖσθαι … τὸ ἀγαθόν) reads 'lies close at hand', matching Romans 7:21 in u05-rem-close and the same verse in u06-open and u06-rem-early, so Paul's repeated verb reads the same across the book.
